title: December 2026 Cold Moon: Exact Date, Viewing Locations & Tips to See the Full Moon
body:
The night sky will be illuminated by a striking full moon on December 13, 2026, offering stargazers a perfect chance to observe the season’s “Cold Moon.” Reaching its peak at 04:24 UTC, the lunar disc will be fully visible across most of the Northern Hemisphere, while the Southern Hemisphere will catch a waning crescent just before sunrise. The event coincides with a quiet stretch of the month’s weather patterns, making it an ideal moment for both casual observers and seasoned astronomers to capture the moon’s crisp, silvery glow against a backdrop of winter constellations.

The Cold Moon, a name rooted in Native American and colonial folklore, reflects the deepening chill of December and the early sunsets that characterize the season. This particular full moon will appear slightly smaller than average because it will occur near the moon’s apogee—its farthest point from Earth—on December 11. At that distance, the lunar diameter will be about 5.5 arcseconds less than at perigee, giving it a subtly “pinprick” appearance that many photographers find appealing. Despite the reduced size, the moon’s brightness will remain formidable, with an apparent magnitude of –12.6, easily outshining any planet or star in the night sky.

Astronomical conditions on December 13 are especially favorable. The moon will rise at 14:31 UTC in Europe and North America, climbing high enough to clear most urban light domes by midnight local time. In the United States, the full moon will be highest in the sky around 19:30 EST, providing a window of roughly three hours of optimal viewing before it begins to set in the west. In contrast, observers in the Southern Hemisphere—particularly in Australia, New Zealand, and South America—will see the moon low on the eastern horizon just before dawn, offering a brief but dramatic silhouette against the emerging sunrise.

For those interested in deeper observation, the December full moon presents several celestial highlights. The moon will be positioned near the constellation Taurus, allowing viewers to spot the bright star Aldebaran just a few degrees to the south. This proximity makes it easy to locate the Hyades star cluster and the Pleiades, the latter of which will be visible in the early evening before the moon’s glare becomes overwhelming. Additionally, the lunar surface will showcase the prominent Mare Serenitatis and the striking crater Tycho, whose bright ejecta rays are best seen when the sun illuminates them at a low angle—conditions that will be met during the moon’s waxing phase a few days before the full.

Amateur astronomers can enhance the experience with modest equipment. A pair of binoculars will reveal the major lunar maria and bright crater rims, while a modest telescope (4‑6 inches aperture) can resolve finer details such as the intricate network of rilles in the crater Plato and the subtle shadows cast by the lunar highlands. Photographers should consider using a fast lens (f/2.8 or wider) and a moderate ISO setting to capture the moon’s texture without overexposing its bright disc. Stacking multiple short exposures can also improve detail and reduce noise, a technique increasingly popular among hobbyists sharing images on social media platforms.

Looking ahead, the Cold Moon marks the final full moon of 2026 and serves as a celestial bookmark before the year’s concluding astronomical events. Within weeks, the planet Mercury will make a close approach to the Sun, and early January will bring a spectacular conjunction of Venus and Jupiter. For those who miss the December 13 peak, the next full moon will arrive on January 12, 2027, offering a fresh canvas for winter skywatching. As the year draws to a close, the Cold Moon reminds us that even amid the longest nights, the universe continues to offer moments of wonder—inviting all who look up to pause, observe, and appreciate the steady rhythm of the cosmos.
